text: Hi, I am Hussein, and this video is about designing a JBoss migrator, a tool that upgrades a legacy Java app to a new server and a new Java version, and proves the business logic in the UI did not change. Here is the ask I started from. Here is the whole idea. The tool migrates the mechanics, namespaces, dependencies, descriptors, and tests. Then it proves nothing else broke. Whatever it cannot do safely, it hands back to you as a list. It starts with three inputs: a get URL, a branch, and a config that declares the upgrade from EAP 7.2 on Java 8 to EAP 8 on Java 17,

Four named upgrades, and the block that matters most, protected paths, the business code in the UI, which the tool may only touch for namespaces, then open a pull request. Six stages, always in this order. Inputs, baseline, analyze, transform, verify, then a test plan, and a pull request. Look where the edits live. Only stage four writes code. Everything before it measures the original app. Everything after it measures the result again. Stage two is the one most migration skip. Before a single change, it clones the repo, cuts a migration branch, builds the original app, and records every test result. Playwright screenshots the key pages. Characterization tests pin what the

Service classes do today. Now, nothing changed to something you can check, not a hope. Analyze takes inventory, the build tool, the dependencies, the deployment descriptors, the server config, and the APIs the code actually calls. Red Hat's Migration Toolkit for Applications already writes this report for EAP upgrades, so the tool runs its command line and parses the issues into a plan. Transform is where each upgrade meets an engine. Open Rewrite does the heavy lifting. Java 17, Jakarta, Hibernate, JUnit. Each is a ready-made recipe that edits the syntax tree, so it changes only what it targets. Eclipse Transformer handles third-party jars. Descriptors get targeted XML rewrites, and the server config becomes JBoss CLI

Scripts. An LLM may propose fixes for leftover errors. But only as suggestions you review. Verify is three checks. A diff guard reads every change inside the protected paths. An import and annotation and namespace allowed. Anything else like this flipped comparison fails the run. Then the baseline tests were run and are compared one by one. Then the app deploys to the target server in a container and its screenshots are compared with the baseline. Last, the paper trail for every changed class, what changed, which recipe changed it, and a risk level. From that, a unit test plan, existing tests mapped, characterization tests included, and gaps flagged for human to write. Then it

Pushes the branch and opens a pull request with the report, the plan, and a list of everything it could not automate. Now the honest part, no tool migrates a real JBoss app 100%. Custom security modules, vendor specific JNDI lookups, and old frameworks like Seam usually need a human. So the design doesn't guess. It automates what is safe, refuses to touch protected code, and hands you a precise list of what is left. So the verdict, measure the app before you change it. Let recipes do the mechanical edits. Put a guard on the business code in the UI and ship a precise list of what is left, not a

Mark each one recipe safe or needs a human and write the characterization test I should run before touching anything. That last clause is the point. Pin today's behavior before anything moves. And the recipe safe list is your migration plan. For one class, prove nothing broke. I am Hussein. Thanks for watching.
